title: Resource optimisation: levelling & smoothing
blurb: Outline the options for resource optimisation, and tell resource levelling (may move the end date) from smoothing (stays within float).
question: Two design activities both need the project's only structural engineer in the same weeks. One has a little float; the other is critical. What options does the project manager have, and which one might push back the end date?

teach.body: A schedule built only on logic can ask for more people than you have. Resource optimisation means making the best use of resources against their availability. The problem it tackles is over-allocation: demand for a resource above what is available, such as one engineer booked onto two jobs at once. A resource histogram shows usage against availability, so peaks jump out.

teach.caption: A simple resource histogram. In weeks 3–4 the only structural engineer is over-allocated.
Ramp design has only one week of float, so shifting it within float still overlaps deck design.

teach.body: Resource levelling resolves over-allocation by delaying activities until the resource is free. Resources are treated as the fixed constraint, so it is also called resource-limited scheduling. Because work can be pushed past its float, levelling MAY EXTEND the project end date, and it can change the critical path. Plainly: 'we only have one engineer, so the job waits, even if we finish later.'

tasks.label: Ramp design
tasks.sub: starts once the engineer is free

teach.caption: The clash is gone, but the end date has moved and ramp design is now on the critical path.

teach.body: Resource smoothing moves activities only within their float to even out resource usage, WITHOUT changing the end date. Time is treated as the fixed constraint, so it is also called time-limited scheduling. Because it can only use the float available, smoothing may not remove every peak. Plainly: 'the date is fixed, so let's shuffle the non-critical work to flatten the peaks as far as we can.'

teach.caption: Moving landscaping later uses its float, so demand never exceeds the four labourers and the opening date stays the same.

items: Add resources: bring in more people or equipment (at a cost).
Substitute resources: use a different person, skill or supplier.
Overtime: extend working hours for a limited period.
Re-sequence: change the order of activities where the logic allows.
Change the scope: reduce or defer work, through change control.

teach.text: The exam swaps these two. LEVELLING can LENGTHEN the project: resources are fixed, the end date may move. SMOOTHING STAYS within float: the end date is fixed, but some peaks may remain. If the question says the deadline cannot move, the answer is smoothing.

items: Resource optimisation: making the best use of resources against their availability.
Levelling: delays activities until resources are free; may extend the end date (resource-limited).
Smoothing: moves activities only within float; end date unchanged (time-limited); may not clear every peak.
Other options: add or substitute resources, overtime, re-sequence, change scope.
A resource histogram shows usage against availability.

summary: You can now outline the options for resource optimisation. You can explain that resource levelling delays work until resources are free and may extend the end date, while resource smoothing moves work only within float and keeps the end date, and you can name the other options such as adding resources, overtime and re-sequencing.

A.q: Which technique moves activities only within their float to even out resource usage?
A.why: Resource smoothing reschedules activities within their float so the end date is not affected.

whyNot.0: Levelling can delay activities beyond their float, which may extend the end date.
whyNot.2: Critical path analysis finds the critical path and float; it doesn't move activities to balance resources.
whyNot.3: Time boxing fixes a period and flexes scope; it isn't a resource balancing technique.

A.q: Complete the statement: resource levelling may ______ the project end date.
A.why: Levelling delays activities until resources are available, which can push the end date out.

whyNot.0: Delaying activities cannot shorten the project.
whyNot.1: Keeping the end date fixed describes smoothing, not levelling.
whyNot.3: An end date can't be removed; it can only move.

A.q: What does a resource histogram show?
options: Who is accountable for each activity
How costs split across work packages
A.why: A resource histogram plots how much of a resource is needed over time against how much is available, revealing peaks and over-allocation.

whyNot.0: Accountability is shown in a responsibility assignment matrix.
whyNot.1: Costs by work package are shown in the cost breakdown structure.
whyNot.2: Dependencies are shown in a network diagram.

B.q: Which of the following best describes resource levelling?
options: Delaying activities until resources are free
Moving activities only within their float
Fixing the end date and dropping the scope
Adding float to activities with high peaks
B.why: Levelling resolves over-allocation by delaying work until the resource is available, even if the end date moves.

whyNot.1: Moving activities only within float describes smoothing.
whyNot.2: Fixing the date and dropping scope describes time boxing.
whyNot.3: Float comes from the network logic; it can't simply be added to activities.

B.q: A new hospital ward must open on a date announced by the health minister, but demand for nurse trainers peaks in week 6. Which technique fits best?
B.why: With a fixed end date, smoothing moves non-critical work within its float to reduce the peak without moving the opening.

whyNot.0: Levelling may extend the end date, which isn't allowed here.
whyNot.1: Analogous estimating produces estimates; it doesn't balance resources.
whyNot.3: Time boxing fixes a period and flexes scope; it is not a resource optimisation technique.

B.q:
Apart from levelling and smoothing, which TWO are options for dealing with over-allocation?
1. Authorise overtime
2. Remove all the float
3. Substitute a different resource
4. Bypass change control
B.why: Overtime and substituting resources are recognised optimisation options, alongside adding resources, re-sequencing and changing scope.

whyNot.0: Float can't simply be removed; it comes from the network logic.
whyNot.2: Neither is an optimisation option, and bypassing change control is never acceptable.
whyNot.3: Scope changes must go through change control, never around it.

C.q: Only one engineer is available, and two design activities need her at once. Smoothing within float can't clear the clash. What is the likely result of levelling?
options: The end date may be pushed back
Her work is removed from scope
C.why: Levelling delays one activity until the engineer is free; if that takes it beyond its float, the end date slips.

whyNot.0: Delaying work can't bring the end date forward.
whyNot.2: Levelling often changes the critical path, as the delayed activity can become critical.
whyNot.3: Levelling reschedules work; it doesn't remove it from scope.

C.q: Which statement about resource smoothing is correct?
options: It always extends the end date
It needs more resources to work
It may not remove every peak
C.why: Smoothing is limited to the float available, so some peaks may remain.

whyNot.0: Smoothing keeps the end date unchanged; that's its defining feature.
whyNot.1: Critical activities have zero float, so smoothing can't move them.
whyNot.2: Smoothing rearranges existing resources; it doesn't need extra ones.

C.q: Resource levelling is also known as which of the following?
C.why: Levelling treats resource availability as the fixed limit, so it is resource-limited scheduling.

whyNot.1: Time-limited scheduling is smoothing, where the end date is fixed.
whyNot.2: Critical path analysis finds the longest path; it isn't levelling.
whyNot.3: Time boxing fixes a period and flexes scope; it isn't levelling.

reteach.title: Think of one bathroom and a busy family morning
reteach.question: Four people need the only bathroom between 7:00 and 7:30. What are your choices?

blocks.h: Wait, or shuffle within the slack
blocks.body: The bathroom is the resource and it's over-allocated. Option one: queue, and accept that the last person leaves the house late (levelling: resources fixed, end time moves). Option two: the teenager who doesn't need to leave until 8:15 showers at 7:45 instead, using their slack, so nobody is late (smoothing: end time fixed, work moved within float). Or you could add a resource: use the downstairs basin.

blocks.text: Levelling Lengthens; Smoothing Stays (within float, end date unchanged).

explain.body: A resource is over-allocated when demand is above availability. A resource histogram shows this as a bar above the availability line. Resource optimisation is about making the best use of resources against their availability.

test.q: A resource is said to be over-allocated when which of the following is true?
options: The activity is on the critical path
test.why: Over-allocation means more of a resource is needed than is available at that time.

whyNot.2: Float is about time, not resource demand.
whyNot.3: Being critical is about time, not resource demand.

explain.body: Levelling delays activities until the resource is free. Resources are the fixed limit, so the end date may be extended and the critical path may change.

test.q: What is the main drawback of resource levelling?
test.why: Delaying work until resources are free can push activities past their float and so extend the end date.

whyNot.0: Levelling usually uses up float rather than creating it.
whyNot.1: Levelling reschedules work; it doesn't require scope cuts.
whyNot.3: Levelling aims to keep resources busy within their availability.

explain.body: Smoothing moves activities only within their float to even out demand. The end date is the fixed limit, so it does not change, but some peaks may remain.

test.q: Resource smoothing protects which of the following?
test.why: Smoothing only uses float, so the project end date stays the same.

whyNot.0: Smoothing works with existing resources; it doesn't protect a number.
whyNot.1: Activities are moved in time; the logic stays, but timing changes.
whyNot.2: Smoothing uses up float rather than protecting it.

explain.body: Besides levelling and smoothing, a PM can add resources, substitute resources, use overtime, re-sequence activities or change scope through change control. Each has a cost or a risk to weigh.

test.q: Which of these is NOT a resource optimisation option?
test.why: The business case justifies the project; rewriting it does nothing to balance resource demand.

whyNot.0: Overtime is a recognised way to increase capacity.
whyNot.2: Re-sequencing can move work away from peaks.
whyNot.3: Adding resources raises availability to meet demand.
